title: Health and the body
objectives: I can name the main parts of the body and say where it hurts.
I can describe symptoms with estar com and doer at the doctor's office or the pharmacy.
I can understand and give simple advice with precisar, ter que, dever and the imperative.
I can use definite articles and reflexive verbs correctly with body parts.
I can talk about health care in Brazil: the SUS, plano de saúde and the pharmacy.

dialogues.title: At the doctor
dialogues.context: Paulo visits Dr. Márcia with a sore throat and a fever.

lines.speaker: Márcia
lines.pt: Bom dia, Paulo. O que você está sentindo?
lines.en: Good morning, Paulo. What are you feeling?

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.pt: Bom dia, doutora. Estou com dor de garganta e tosse há três dias.
lines.en: Good morning, doctor. I have had a sore throat and a cough for three days.

lines.speaker: Márcia
lines.pt: Você está com febre?
lines.en: Do you have a fever?

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.pt: Estou. Ontem à noite deu trinta e oito graus.
lines.en: I do. Last night it was thirty-eight degrees.

lines.speaker: Márcia
lines.pt: Onde dói mais? A garganta ou o peito?
lines.en: Where does it hurt more? The throat or the chest?

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.pt: Dói mais a garganta. Também estou com dor no corpo.
lines.en: The throat hurts more. I also have body aches.

lines.speaker: Márcia
lines.pt: Abra a boca e diga ah. A garganta está muito vermelha. Você está com uma infecção.
lines.en: Open your mouth and say ah. Your throat is very red. You have an infection.

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.pt: Preciso tomar algum remédio?
lines.en: Do I need to take some medicine?

lines.speaker: Márcia
lines.pt: Vou passar um antibiótico. Tome um comprimido de oito em oito horas por sete dias.
lines.en: I will prescribe an antibiotic. Take one pill every eight hours for seven days.

lines.speaker: Paulo
lines.pt: Posso trabalhar?
lines.en: Can I work?

lines.speaker: Márcia
lines.pt: Não. Descanse, beba bastante água e não tome nada frio. Vou te dar um atestado de três dias.
lines.en: No. Rest, drink plenty of water and do not have anything cold. I will give you a three-day note.

dialogues.title: At the pharmacy
dialogues.context: Carlos has a headache and a stuffy nose and asks the pharmacist Lúcia for advice.

lines.speaker: Lúcia
lines.pt: Boa tarde! Posso ajudar?
lines.en: Good afternoon! May I help?

lines.speaker: Carlos
lines.pt: Boa tarde. Estou com dor de cabeça desde ontem e o nariz está entupido. O que você recomenda?
lines.en: Good afternoon. I have had a headache since yesterday and my nose is stuffy. What do you recommend?

lines.speaker: Lúcia
lines.pt: Você está com febre?
lines.en: Do you have a fever?

lines.speaker: Carlos
lines.pt: Não, só um pouco de cansaço. Acho que é um resfriado.
lines.en: No, just a little tiredness. I think it is a cold.

lines.speaker: Lúcia
lines.pt: Então leve este remédio pra gripe. Tome um comprimido de seis em seis horas.
lines.en: Then take this flu medicine. Take one pill every six hours.

lines.speaker: Carlos
lines.pt: Preciso de receita?
lines.en: Do I need a prescription?

lines.speaker: Lúcia
lines.pt: Não precisa. Mas, depois de três dias, procure um médico.
lines.en: You do not. But after three days, see a doctor.

lines.speaker: Carlos
lines.pt: E pra tosse? Minha tosse também não passa.
lines.en: And for the cough? My cough will not go away either.

lines.speaker: Lúcia
lines.pt: Leve também um xarope. E beba bastante água e não saia no frio.
lines.en: Take a syrup too. And drink plenty of water and do not go out in the cold.

lines.speaker: Carlos
lines.pt: Tá bom. Posso pagar com cartão?
lines.en: Okay. Can I pay by card?

dialogues.title: A twisted foot
dialogues.context: Igor notices that his friend Rafaela is limping after a workout.

lines.speaker: Igor
lines.pt: Rafa, você está mancando. O que aconteceu?
lines.en: Rafa, you are limping. What happened?

lines.speaker: Rafaela
lines.pt: Torci o pé no treino ontem. Agora dói o pé e o joelho também.
lines.en: I twisted my foot at practice yesterday. Now my foot hurts, and my knee too.

lines.speaker: Igor
lines.pt: Você foi ao médico?
lines.en: Did you go to the doctor?

lines.speaker: Rafaela
lines.pt: Fui ao posto de saúde hoje cedo. Esperei duas horas, mas o médico foi ótimo.
lines.en: I went to the health clinic early today. I waited two hours, but the doctor was great.

lines.speaker: Igor
lines.pt: O que ele disse?
lines.en: What did he say?

lines.speaker: Rafaela
lines.pt: Disse que eu não devo correr por duas semanas. Tenho que fazer repouso e pôr gelo no pé três vezes por dia.
lines.en: He said I should not run for two weeks. I have to rest and put ice on my foot three times a day.

lines.speaker: Igor
lines.pt: Então não treine amanhã, hein?
lines.en: Then do not work out tomorrow, okay?

lines.speaker: Rafaela
lines.pt: Pode deixar. Vou só assistir a séries e descansar.
lines.en: Rest assured. I will just watch series and rest.

lines.speaker: Igor
lines.pt: Quer uma sopa? Eu levo pra você.
lines.en: Do you want some soup? I will bring it to you.

lines.speaker: Rafaela
lines.pt: Quero! Obrigada.
lines.en: Yes! Thank you.

grammar.title: Dói, doem and estar com: describing pain and symptoms
grammar.explanation:
Doer (to hurt) is normally used only in the third person: dói for one thing and doem for more than one. The body part is the grammatical subject, so the verb agrees with it: Dói a cabeça, Doem os pés. The body part can also come first: A cabeça dói, Os pés doem. Formally, an indirect pronoun shows who feels the pain (Me dói a cabeça, Lhe dói o joelho), but in daily speech people prefer a possessive or the progressive: Minha cabeça está doendo, Está doendo o meu joelho. To ask where, say Onde dói? and to answer, Dói aqui.

For symptoms the most common structure is estar com plus a noun: Estou com febre, Estou com tosse, Estou com dor de cabeça, Estou com dor nas costas. Ter also works: Tenho febre. Use de after dor for head, throat, teeth, ear, stomach and belly (dor de cabeça, dor de garganta, dor de dente, dor de ouvido, dor de barriga) and the contraction no, na, nos, nas for most other places (dor no peito, dor nas costas, dor no joelho).

For illnesses, use estar plus the adjective: Estou gripado, Estou resfriado, Estou doente, Estou com gripe.

rows: estar com dor no, na, nos, nas + place

grammar.title: Advice with precisar, ter que and dever
grammar.explanation:
To give advice or say what someone must do, Portuguese uses a conjugated verb followed by an infinitive. Precisar means 'need to' and is friendly and natural: Você precisa descansar. Ter que means 'have to' and is stronger: Você tem que ir ao médico. Dever means 'should' or 'ought to': Você deve beber mais água. In the negative, não deve means 'should not' and is a recommendation, but não precisa means 'you do not need to' and não tem que means 'you do not have to'.

Another very common frame is É melhor plus an infinitive: É melhor ficar em casa. Note that the infinitive does not change: Eu preciso descansar, Nós temos que esperar, Eles devem tomar o remédio.

Be careful with precisar: before an infinitive it has no preposition (preciso descansar), but before a noun it takes de (preciso de um remédio, preciso de receita). In casual speech, Tem que plus an infinitive is often used impersonally: Tem que tomar esse remédio.

rows: Você tem que tomar o remédio.
Você não precisa ir ao hospital.

grammar.title: The imperative for advice: tome, não coma
grammar.explanation:
Doctors, pharmacists and friends often give advice with the imperative. For você, start with the eu form of the present, remove the final -o and add the opposite vowel: -ar verbs take -e (tomo becomes tome) and -er and -ir verbs take -a (como becomes coma, abro becomes abra). The same form is used with vocês: tomem, comam. For a negative command, put não before the same verb: Não tome, Não coma.

Spelling follows the sound: verbs in -car and -gar change the consonant (ficar: fique, pagar: pague), fazer gives faça because the eu form is faço, and dormir gives durma because the eu form is durmo. Since the imperative is built from the present of the eu form, irregular verbs such as sair (saio) give saia.

In casual speech, many Brazilians use the ordinary present as a soft command (Toma esse remédio, Bebe água), especially among friends and family. Pronouns such as me and te go before the verb in speech: Me avisa!, Me liga!, while in instructions from a professional the pure imperative forms are the norm. The next units expand on this.

grammar.title: Body parts with articles and reflexive verbs
grammar.explanation:
When Portuguese speakers talk about their own body, they normally use the definite article instead of a possessive, because the owner is already clear. English says 'I broke my leg', but Portuguese says Quebrei a perna. 'Wash your hands' is Lave as mãos, and 'He hurt his knee' is Ele machucou o joelho. Using a possessive here is correct, but it can sound heavy, and it is normally saved for emphasis, contrast or another person's body: O médico examinou a minha garganta.

For actions you do to yourself, Portuguese often uses a reflexive pronoun placed before the verb in Brazilian speech: Eu me cortei, Ele se queimou, Ela se machucou. If the body part is named, the reflexive is often dropped and the article takes over: Cortei o dedo, Machuquei o joelho. Both are natural, but you do not need both the pronoun and the possessive.

In health contexts, use ficar for change of state (Fiquei gripado), estar for the present condition (Estou cansado), and doer for pain. Note the plural forms: a mão and as mãos, o pé and os pés, as costas (always plural).

culture.title: SUS, planos de saúde and the farmácia
culture.text:
Brazil has one of the largest public health systems in the world, the SUS (Sistema Único de Saúde). It is free for everyone, including foreigners, and covers everything from vaccines and routine appointments at the posto de saúde to emergency care and complex surgeries. Many people also pay for a plano de saúde, a private insurance which usually gives faster access to specialists. For urgent cases there are UPAs, open 24 hours, and the pronto-socorro of hospitals. The emergency number for an ambulance is 192 (SAMU), and 193 is the fire department.

The farmácia plays a bigger role than in many countries. Pharmacists often recommend medicine for simple problems such as headache, cold or stomach upset, and most farmácias also apply injections and measure blood pressure. Antibiotics, however, require a receita. Big chains are open until late and some are open 24 hours, and many delivery apps bring medicine to your home. Generic medicines, called genéricos, are usually much cheaper than name brands.

Home remedies are also part of the culture. People drink chá de erva-doce, chá de camomila or chá de boldo for stomach ailments, and honey with lemon for a sore throat. If you are sick, you are likely to hear Melhoras! (Get well soon) or Se cuida! (Take care). The vaccination campaigns of the SUS have a famous mascot, Zé Gotinha, a little drop with a smiling face that children know well.

paragraphs.pt: A gripe é muito comum no inverno. Para evitar, lave as mãos várias vezes por dia e não coloque a mão no rosto. Beba bastante água e durma pelo menos sete horas por noite.
paragraphs.en: The flu is very common in winter. To avoid it, wash your hands several times a day and do not put your hand on your face. Drink plenty of water and sleep at least seven hours a night.

paragraphs.pt: Se você já está com gripe, fique em casa e descanse. Tome chá quente e evite sair quando faz frio. Depois de três dias com febre, procure um médico no posto de saúde mais perto.
paragraphs.en: If you already have the flu, stay home and rest. Drink hot tea and avoid going out when it is cold. After three days with a fever, see a doctor at the nearest health clinic.
